implementation_notes: The TypeScript realization is a test-support module of typed factories - 'const createCustomer = (overrides: Partial<Customer> = {}): Customer => ({...defaults, ...overrides})' - where the declared return type is the domain type, so a mother that drifts from the model fails to compile. Partial<T>/DeepPartial<T> express overrides without weakening the factory's contract, and object spread applies them. Types do not make the data valid: keep invariant-bearing defaults in the factory and use fishery when typed params, sequences or associations are needed.
pitfalls: Partial<T> only makes fields optional; it cannot express cross-field invariants, so an override can still build a domain-invalid object.
Spread is shallow: overriding address replaces the whole nested object instead of merging, silently dropping fields the test still relies on.
Deep-partial helpers rely on conditional mapped types and casts; if the factory's return type widens to any or a structural supertype, compile-time drift detection is lost.
Using ?? instead of spread for overrides makes falsy-but-valid values (0, '', false) silently fall back to the default.

variants.name: Typed declarative factories with fishery
variants.idiom_name: Factory.define<T>() with typed params and build() overlays
variants.implementation_notes: fishery is built with TypeScript in mind: Factory.define<User>(({sequence, params}) => ...) declares the factory, build({...}) takes a DeepPartial<User> overlay, and transient params/associations cover cases a plain factory function would need extra arguments for. Adopt it once the suite has many fixtures or needs sequences, and keep plain typed functions for the handful of canonical examples.
pitfalls: DeepPartial params let nested overrides replace whole subtrees; the same shallow-merge surprise as with spread.
build() overlays are unvalidated: type errors are caught, domain invariants are not.
Sequence-based ids make fixtures order-dependent when test files run in parallel within one process.
